newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico coffee trade plunders stocks for record Jan.
newsitem.headline: Mexico coffee trade plunders stocks for record Jan.

text.p: Mexican coffee traders plundered bean stocks in January from the 1996-1997 harvest to achieve an all-time monthly record export level, exporters and traders said Wednesday.
"The exports broke all previous monthly records and was all because of the spike in prices," Jenaro Hernandez, the executive director of the Mexican Coffee Exporters' Association said.
Mexican coffee exports in January outstripped the same month a year earlier by 17.5 percent or 130,476 60-kg bags, the Mexican Coffee Council said Tuesday.

The council, Mexico's umbrella organization for the whole sector, said exports in the month were a whopping 875,904 60-kg bags compared to the 745,428 bags in January 1996, a figure that was itself the record for the past five cycles.
"When the month starts at around $116 per 100 lb and ends the month at $144, which is a 24 percent rise, people are going to sell what they have," Hernandez said.

"All the coffee that was in stock in Mexico was sold in January," he said. He calculated that to the end of the current cycle (February to September) another 1.3 million bags would be exported from Mexico.

Such a figure would take Mexican exports for the cycle to 3 million bags, a huge dip from the 4.5 million bags exported from the 1995-1996 cycle, although closer to the 1994-1995 exports of 3.3 million bags.

In the first four months of the October-September 1996-1997 cycle (October through January), Mexico has exported 1,750,379 bags compared to 1,565,295 bags in the same four month period, up 185,084 bags, or an 11.8 percent hike.
Ernesto Gutierrez, manager of the Tuxtla Gutierrez-based trading and exporting company Cafe de Chiapas, said the export figure was surprising despite the surge in prices.
"It is surprising given the crop in Veracruz state is well down this year and the crop in Chiapas, without being very bad, is not good either," Gutierrez said.
He added he saw the Mexican harvest finishing much earlier this cycle than most other expectations.

Gutierrez also pointed out European nations were showing strong demand for Mexican coffees and pushing down differentials (the punitive pricing slapped on Mexican coffees) from previous years and generally below differentials offered by U.S. traders.

He said normally around 10 percent of Mexican exports were shipped out of Veracruz port to Europe but this cycle he saw that percentage rising to between 30 and 40 percent. "The Americans will have to bear that in mind if they are planning to top up with Mexican coffee later in the year," he said.
Another trader, who declined to be named, said Mexico was still taking advantage of the export limits in place for nations belonging to the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC).
"With other countries having to stick to quarterly exports limits for the ACPC, Mexican beans have been in demand because they are free of restraints," he said.
